source.title: jailbreaking leading safety-aligned LLMs with simple adaptive attacks
source.authors: Maksym Andriushchenko; Francesco Croce; Nicolas Flammarion

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether adaptive suffix and response-prefilling attacks can bypass refusal, using attack-success rates rather than measuring aligned-versus-base per-token KL or fine-tuning effects.
record.gate_note: The paper reports harmful-compliance attack-success rates for its own prompting, random-search suffix, transfer, and prefilling attacks. Rows below cover those results and selected prompt-structure variations. Comparisons attributed to prior work are not recorded as this study's results.
record.test_reason: The study measures harmful-compliance attack-success rates on safety-aligned models under two kinds of attack. One is adversarial suffixes, found by random search on first-token 'Sure' logprob or transferred from GPT-4. The other is prefilling the assistant's response with a compliant start. This is a different method from the originals aimed at V4. It is not an original source. It does not fine-tune models or measure per-token KL, so it tests no other version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors also claim 100% attack success, under the GPT-4 judge, on all leading safety-aligned models tested. They state that these models are completely non-robust, that adaptive model-specific attacks are necessary, and that no single method works across all targets.
record.recipe_differences: This study uses adaptive jailbreak prompts, logprob-guided random search, suffix transfer, and response prefilling. It does not reproduce fine-tuning effects or aligned-versus-base per-token KL measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: Attack success varies by model, prompt template, request-message structure, and restart count. The authors report that the standard prompt and self-transfer perform poorly on some models, while custom prompts, in-context examples, system-message placement, suffix search, or prefilling can change outcomes.
record.problems: The main harmful-request evaluations use 50 requests and primarily rely on GPT-4 as a semantic judge. The authors report multiple GPT-4 judge false positives for Claude 2.1 and acknowledge that a high jailbreak score does not always mean the output is practically useful. Results also vary substantially across models and attack configurations.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted the remaining Claude prompt-structure and restart-count combinations from Tables 15–17, other judge-by-model values from Tables 20 and 22, and convergence-curve values in Figure 2. These add further condition-specific attack-success results or judge comparisons beyond the selected rows; the paper's cited baseline results were also left out.

untested.parts: No per-token KL between aligned and base models.
Decoding changes are not tested. The paper also does not test prefill depth or how many tokens of prefill are needed.
No analysis of the causes of shallowness.
No deepening training. Defenses are mentioned only in discussion.

missing.what: Assistant-only prefill at 10 restarts: 54% to 98% across Claude models (e.g. Haiku 98%, Opus 96%, 3.5 Sonnet 66%). Other prefill structures: user+assistant and system+assistant.

Prefill with system+user+assistant at 1 restart for the other Claude models (e.g. 3.5 Sonnet 100%, Opus 76%, Haiku 96%) against system+user without prefill (0–48%). These form the cleanest prefill-vs-no-prefill contrast.
Transfer-attack success by restart count and message structure, including Claude Instant 1.2 (54%) and Claude 2.1 at 0% throughout.
Judge sensitivity for the strongest attacks: rule-based 90–98%, Llama Guard 2 86–96%. Llama-2-7B in-context+RS+ST gives 76% under GPT-4 but 16% under the rule-based judge.
On 100 JailbreakBench behaviors with the Llama-3-70B judge, Prompt+RS+ST gives Llama-2-7B 90%, GPT-4 Turbo 78%, GPT-3.5 93%.
Random search on the default template gives little gain on GPT-4o; stated in the text without a number.

record.verdict_notes: The template-only, in-context-only and non-aligned-model rows were moved to 'none' because they involve no suffix or prefill, or no safety training. The random search objective is the first response token's logprob, which fits V4's opening-token mechanism, but the study never measures token-position effects. The Claude prefill results combine the prefill with a jailbreak prompt. Pure prefill is weaker, so the 100% figures overstate what prefilling alone achieves. Most results use 50 requests and a GPT-4 judge, with no uncertainty reported.

versions.untested_parts: Does not fine-tune models on harmful examples or measure refusal after such fine-tuning.
Does not fine-tune models on benign data or measure changes in harmful compliance after benign fine-tuning.
Does not measure per-token KL divergence between aligned and base models.
Tests adversarial suffix, transfer, and response-prefilling attacks. Does not test decoding changes.
Does not test whether safety is localized in a small set of weights or ranks.
Does not test what data or training objective produces shallowness.
Does not test training to deepen safety or whether such training holds up.
